messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Medical Record Number: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 50-year-old Asian woman, was admitted to our hospital due to sudden anterior chest pain. Hematology, biochemistry, and blood gas analyses were performed and found to be normal. A chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a ground-glass opacity (GGO) in her left S10 lung segment and a solitary small nodule in her left S4 segment. Further testing was carried out, which led to suspicion of lung carcinoma. However, the patient did not provide consent for surgical resection.

After follow-up with CT scans, it was suggested that the GGO was lung carcinoma, and a pathological diagnosis was established through a left lower lobectomy and an upper lung partial resection. The cancer was identified as primary lung adenocarcinoma (localized bronchioloalveolar carcinoma).

There was also a small nodule in her left S4, which was initially suspected to be lung metastasis, however, it was later discovered to be a benign metastasizing leiomyoma (BML). The patient had a history of undergoing a total abdominal hysterectomy for uterine leiomyoma in the past, which is why the small nodule was identified as BML.

Management and Outcome:
No additional therapy was given, and the patient was monitored by follow-up chest CT scans over four years. No recurrence of lung cancer or BML could be detected throughout her follow-up.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Instructions:
The patient is advised to continue her follow-up with her physician and have periodic screening of the chest CT scans.

Scheduled Follow-up Appointments:
Follow-up screening every six months for two years and then annually.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the episode of care is the primary lung adenocarcinoma (localized bronchioloalveolar carcinoma). It was confirmed pathologically and treated by left lower lobectomy. This belongs to chapter C (neoplasms), category C34 (malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung). The benign metastasizing leiomyoma is a secondary finding.

CODE: C34
